title: Variance and Advanced Generics
summary: The finer points of generics - why a List<Cat> is not a List<Animal>, covariance with out and contravariance with in, which built-in interfaces and delegates are variant, writing variant interfaces of your own, default(T), static data per closed generic type, generic caches, and constraints for enums, delegates and unmanaged types.

cards.q: Why is `IEnumerable<Cat>` usable as `IEnumerable<Animal>` but `List<Cat>` is not usable as `List<Animal>`?
cards.a:
`IEnumerable<out T>` only gives items out; `List<T>` also takes items in, so it must stay invariant

If a `List<Cat>` were a `List<Animal>`, you could add a dog to it. A sequence you can only read from has no such risk, so it is covariant; no copy is made.

cards.q: How many copies of a static field in `Box<T>` exist after using `Box<int>` and `Box<string>`?
cards.a:
Two: each closed generic type has its own static fields

`Box<int>` and `Box<string>` are different types at run time, and each has its own copy of the static field.

IEnumerable<object> e = new List<string>();

IEnumerable is covariant for reference types. List is invariant, and variance does not apply to int.
